sources.news_title: US Fed holds interest rates at 3.9% as inflation remains high
sources.text:
The Federal Reserve kept its key rate unchanged Wednesday at about 3.9 per cent despite stubbornly high inflation, while providing little hint about the central bank’s next moves.
“Inflation remains elevated,” the Fed said in a statement released after its two-day policy meeting. Holding off on an increase will allow “the accumulation of more information” that will help determine what policy the Fed should pursue “to ensure a timely return of inflation” to the central bank’s 2 per cent inflation target, the statement said.
The Fed, led by Chairman Kevin Warsh, raised its benchmark rate last month for the first time in three years, defying President Donald Trump’s demands for rate cuts, in an effort to get inflation back to its 2 per cent target in a “timelier” manner. The Fed is tasked by Congress to combat inflation, and it does so by lifting rates to slow borrowing and spending and cool price increases.
The statement leaves the Fed’s next moves unclear, even though officials last month penciled in another rate hike for this year. Wall Street investors have also priced in a rate hike in December, according to futures markets. Whether the Fed is still leaning toward another hike will likely be a key issue in the news conference held by Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh this afternoon.
The Fed’s decision comes just six days before a midterm election that has focused heavily on concerns around the cost of living and affordability. Consumers have generally soured on an economy weighed down by more expensive gas, groceries, and clothing, among other items. Yet Warsh faces plenty of challenges in getting inflation back to target. Some of the forces pushing up prices — specifically the rapid buildout of artificial intelligence infrastructure and higher energy prices — won’t easily be tamed by higher interest rates.
Two Fed officials dissented from Wednesday’s decision, with Fed governor Lisa Cook and Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland President Beth Hammack voting in favor of hiking rates by a quarter point. This is Cook’s first dissent since she was appointed to the board by President Joe Biden in 2022.
Cook has been targeted by the Trump administration, which tried to fire her last year, though the Supreme Court in June ruled she could keep her job while litigation played out. No president has fired a Fed governor before, a sign of the Fed’s longstanding independence from day-to-day politics. Trump renewed his attempt to remove Cook last month by setting up a committee to look into allegations Cook committed mortgage fraud, which she has denied.
President Trump has also slammed the Fed for raising its key rate last month, though he largely blamed the central bank’s rate-setting committee, rather than Warsh, whom he appointed.
Other parts of the economy are already being hit by higher rates, which were lifted by market forces, even before the Fed hiked last month. The average 30-year mortgage rate reached a three-year high of 7.4 per cent earlier this month, though it has since slipped a bit. Higher mortgage rates have made buying a home unaffordable for 5 million more Americans since the beginning of the year, according to Oxford Economics, a consulting firm. Over time, Fed rate hikes can make mortgages, auto loans, and credit card borrowing more expensive, adding to Americans’ sense that things like homes and cars are getting pricier.
Inflation picked up in September, when consumer prices rose 3.7 per cent compared with a year earlier. The increase was much bigger than the 2.4 per cent rate in February, just before the Iran war.
And on a monthly basis, the consumer price index — the most widely followed inflation gauge — rose 0.3 per cent in both August and September. At that pace over a full year, inflation would rise much more quickly than the Fed’s 2 per cent target.
A separate inflation measure more closely followed by the Fed, the personal consumption expenditures price index, comes out Thursday and is forecast to have jumped 3.6 per cent in September from a year earlier, up from 3.4 per cent in August. Core prices, which exclude the food and energy categories, are forecast to have risen 3.1 per cent, up from 3 per cent the previous month.
The Fed’s policy meeting is part of a busy week for central banks around the world. The Bank of Canada will also meet Wednesday and is forecast to lift its key rate a quarter point, to 2.5 per cent. Policymakers at the European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan are both scheduled to meet Thursday and are expected to keep their key rates unchanged.
For Warsh and the Fed, another key consideration is that the US economy is growing at a healthy pace and unemployment remains low, at 4.2 per cent, even if hiring is also sluggish. The government will report Thursday on growth for the July-September quarter, which is expected to reach 3 per cent, according to a forecast by data provider FactSet. That would be up from 2.2 per cent in the April-June quarter.
Many economists argue that solid growth is evidence that interest rates aren’t particularly high and the economy could withstand higher rates to combat inflation.

sources.news_title: Fed Holds Rates at 3.75%–4% as Inflation Keeps Pressure on Household Budgets
sources.text:
WASHINGTON — The Federal Reserve left its benchmark interest rate unchanged Wednesday, keeping the target range at 3.75% to 4% as policymakers weigh stubborn inflation against an economy they described as growing at a strong pace.
The Federal Open Market Committee approved the decision by a 10–2 vote at the close of its Oct. 27–28 meeting. Fed Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented, preferring a quarter-percentage-point increase, according to the Fed’s official statement.
The hold follows a quarter-point increase in September, the first rate hike in more than three years. In Wednesday’s statement, officials said domestic spending has remained resilient, productivity growth is strong and capital investment is robust. At the same time, they acknowledged that inflation remains above the central bank’s 2% goal and said additional data will guide the next policy move.
Fed Chair Kevin Warsh told reporters that policymakers do not believe the economy is overheating. He said the central bank aims to restore price stability without unnecessarily slowing growth or increasing unemployment, according to Reuters’ coverage of the press conference. Warsh also said politics played no role in the decision, which came less than a week before the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
What the pause means for households
The federal funds rate does not directly set mortgage, auto-loan or credit-card rates, but it strongly influences borrowing costs across the economy. Wednesday’s decision therefore offers no immediate policy-driven relief for families carrying variable-rate debt or preparing to finance a home or vehicle.
Mortgage rates have already climbed sharply. The Associated Press reported that the average 30-year mortgage rate reached a three-year high of 7.4% earlier in October before easing somewhat. Credit-card interest rates and many other consumer borrowing costs also tend to remain elevated when the Fed’s benchmark rate is high.
For Houston-area families, the result is a continued squeeze from both sides: prices remain high while financing major purchases is expensive. A pause avoids another immediate rate increase, but it does not lower monthly payments for most borrowers.
Another decision is coming in December
Two dissenting votes in favor of a hike show that pressure for tighter policy remains inside the central bank. The Fed’s next rate-setting meeting is scheduled for Dec. 8–9. Before then, officials will review new readings on inflation, employment and economic growth.
The Fed’s preferred inflation measure, the personal consumption expenditures price index, is due Thursday. That report and the data that follow will help determine whether policymakers keep rates steady again or resume increases before the end of the year.

sources.news_title: Fed leaves rates unchanged as it awaits ‘more information’, delays changes until after US midterms
sources.text:
Fed leaves rates unchanged as it awaits ‘more information’, delays changes until after US midterms
The US central bank will maintain its benchmark interest rate within the current 3.75% to 4% range
[WASHINGTON] The US Federal Reserve held interest rates steady on Wednesday (Oct 28), as expected, opting to delay any changes to borrowing costs until after next week’s US midterm elections and awaiting further data on the path of inflation.
In a 10-2 decision, the US central bank said it would maintain its benchmark interest rate within the current 3.75 to 4 per cent range while acknowledging that inflation “remains elevated”, upgrading its assessment of the economy, and hinting that further rate hikes may be coming depending on the performance of inflation.
“The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee’s 2 per cent goal,” the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee said in its latest policy statement. “The Committee will deliver price stability.”
Fed chairman Kevin Warsh, speaking in a press conference following the end of the policy meeting, did not offer guidance on the outlook for monetary policy, but acknowledged that the central bank had not achieved price stability. “We’re working on it,” he said.
Warsh, who took over as head of the central bank in May, added that he does not believe “in prejudging meetings” and noted that “a lot of things can happen, so I’m not going to be able to share with you my musings about what happens when this group gets together six weeks from now”.
Fed governor Lisa Cook, currently being targeted by US President Donald Trump for removal from the central bank, cast her first dissent on a central bank policy decision, favouring a quarter-percentage-point rate hike.
Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack, a consistently hawkish voice, also dissented in favour of the same rate increase.
The Fed’s latest policy statement is a notable change from the September 15-16 meeting, with a hint of the sort of forward guidance Warsh has said he wants to avoid.
The central bank’s assessment of the economy was upgraded to “strong” from the “solid” expansion seen as of the September meeting, while investment was still described as robust and job gains were viewed as keeping pace with the workforce.
Market reaction was muted, with US stocks paring gains slightly after the decision. US Treasury yields extended their rise, with the 10-year Treasury note yield at 5.042 per cent. Short-term interest rate futures rose a bit, as traders pulled back a bit on bets of Fed rate hikes ahead.
“A hold isn’t relief,” said Kelly Brown, the CEO of Ampersand, a deposit management company. “It’s the Fed telling Main Street to wait. With inflation still at 3.7 per cent, and oil above US$100 a barrel, businesses can’t count on borrowing costs coming down anytime soon.”
Fears that inflation is broadening
The outcome of this week’s meeting was widely expected after top Fed officials indicated they saw no rush to raise rates again following the quarter-percentage-point increase approved in September, despite inflation data in the meantime that was stronger than forecast and concerns that price pressures are broadening across the economy.
Energy costs remain high, including for diesel fuel, which is a key input for shipping, agriculture, and other industries.
Inflation and the cost of living in general have been central to the political races that will determine whether Trump’s Republican Party remains in control of both houses of Congress on Nov 3, or whether Democrats move into leadership positions and gain more robust oversight powers, including over the Fed.
Financial markets are still pricing in a couple of additional rate hikes in the coming months, though with slightly less conviction than before Warsh spoke on Wednesday.
Pricing shows about an 80 per cent chance of a rate hike at the Fed’s December 8-9 meeting, with another likely by March.
Inflation, which is currently around a percentage point above the Fed’s target, has shown little progress in recent months.
The US central bank has missed its inflation target for five and a half years, a fact that has left some officials worried that businesses and households are becoming accustomed to faster price increases and may plan for them in ways that will make inflation harder to control. REUTERS

sources.news_title: US Fed holds interest rates steady despite ‘too high’ inflation
sources.text:
The 12-member Federal Open Market Committee voted 10-2 to hold rates at a target range between 3.75 to 4.00 percent, citing the need for more data in the fight against inflation, after having hiked for the first time in three years at its previous meeting in September.
Two members of the committee, Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented, calling instead for an immediate quarter-point rate hike.
“Energy and related prices have moved higher again in recent weeks, and our job is to ensure that relative price changes in some sectors do not broaden out across the economy,” Warsh told reporters.
Still, he said the FOMC needed more information in the coming weeks to “determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the two-percent goal.”
The committee is scheduled to meet again in early December.
‘Politics played no role’
The central bank has missed its inflation target for more than five years, with households and businesses battered by sustained price increases.
US President Donald Trump’s war on Iran, launched in late February, has sent energy prices skyrocketing and fueled domestic inflation, alongside his wide-ranging tariff policies.
Prices have also been driven by an investment boom in artificial intelligence (AI) technology and the build-out of huge data centers to support it.
The decision comes six days ahead of the Nov 3 midterm elections, in which the Democratic Party is seeking to wrest control of both houses of Congress from Trump’s Republicans.
Trump’s handling of the economy has been a key issue throughout the campaign, with working-class households across the country struggling to make ends meet despite largely stable overall economic growth.
US consumer inflation came in hotter than expected in September, clocking in at 3.7%, edging back towards a three-year high established in May.
“Politics played no role in the decision,” said Warsh, who has insisted that he supports the Fed’s independence despite repeated attacks on the institution by Trump since he took office.
Speaking to broadcaster CNBC after the Fed’s meeting, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said he and Trump had “great confidence” in Warsh.
“I have great confidence in Chair Warsh to steer the Fed between the right combination of growth and inflation because what you don’t want to do is cause enough of a growth slowdown that energy consumption would drop,” he said.
‘Strong’ economic growth
On Wednesday, the Fed said economic activity in the US was expanding at a “strong” pace, upgrading its language from the FOMC meeting six weeks prior.
At his press conference, Warsh spoke to that theme, and questioned whether the AI-led investment boom was fuelling inflation.
“Is the economy running too hot? Is the economy running too strong? That isn’t the judgment of most of my colleagues,” he said.
In a significant move, Warsh also announced that the Fed would be reducing the number of times it sets interest rates in the next two years.
It will continue to meet eight times a year in 2027 and 2028, but will only set interest rates seven times next year and six times the year after that.
“Getting policy right involves assessing near-term developments at timely, regular, and information-rich intervals,” said Warsh.
“But it’s equally important we reserve time and space as an intellectually diverse group for strategic deliberations, for thinking anew about big questions, looking out over longer time horizons.”
‘Don’t understand the logic’
Wendy Edelberg, senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, told AFP before the meeting that a decision to hold after raising rates in September was potentially contradictory, given the labor market — the Fed’s other mandate — has been largely stable.
“In terms of the economics of it, I don’t totally understand the logic,” she said.
“If there was a reason to raise interest rates at the last meeting, I think that there’s just as compelling of an economic reason to raise interest rates at this meeting.”
The Fed has a dual mandate to maintain maximum employment while keeping inflation to its long-term target.
It achieves this goal largely using one tool: the economy’s key interest rate. Raising rates tends to cool inflation but can also dampen economic activity; lowering them can spur economic activity but also fuel inflation.
The US unemployment rate has been largely stable around 4.2% over the last year, with job growth mostly in positive territory — albeit driven by a few sectors.
Other advanced economies have also been grappling with high inflation, and on Wednesday Canada’s central bank raised its key rate to 2.5%, its first hike since July 2023.

sources.news_title: Fed pause won’t lower mortgage rates, economists say
sources.text:
Original article can be found here.
(The Center Square) – The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady Wednesday, a decision that does little for homebuyers facing mortgage rates near 7.3% and builder confidence that is at a 14-year low.
The Federal Open Market Committee kept its benchmark rate at 3.75% to 4% on a 10-2 vote, according to the Fed’s policy statement. Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented, preferring a quarter-point increase. September’s decision was unanimous.
The rate that prices a mortgage is not the one the Fed sets. The 10-year Treasury yield, which mortgage rates track, traded just above 5% Wednesday afternoon, according to Tradeweb data. Freddie Mac put the average 30-year fixed mortgage at 7.32% last week, up from 6.19% a year earlier. That is a gap of more than a full percentage point built up over a year in which the Fed raised short-term rates once.
“For homebuyers, today’s decision changes very little,” said Orphe Divounguy, The Center Square’s economist. “The Fed doesn’t directly set mortgage rates. Financial markets do, based on expectations for inflation, economic growth, future interest rates and the risks associated with mortgage-backed securities.”
His research found that about half of a change in the 10-year Treasury yield reaches mortgage rates the same day, and about two-thirds within two days.
Builder confidence fell three points to 29 in October, the lowest reading since June 2012, according to the National Association of Home Builders/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index.
Buyer traffic dropped to 18, which National Association of Home Builders Chief Economist Robert Dietz said in the NAHB’s Oct. 19 release was the weakest since April 2012, excluding the start of the pandemic. Margins are being compressed by rising costs and incentive use, Dietz told The Center Square.
Forty-three percent of builders cut prices last month, the highest share since 2020, and 65% offered sales incentives.
In written commentary after the decision, Mortgage Bankers Association Chief Economist Mike Fratantoni said rates at three-year highs are “causing a sharp slowdown in home sales, mortgage originations, and in commercial real estate markets.”
Although the Fed held Wednesday, he said, markets have already priced in at least two more increases, and “we do not expect any significant relief in mortgage rates over the forecast horizon.”
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said tighter financial conditions are how the policy is meant to work.
“The dominant means in which this policy is going to be put into practice is we are tightening financial conditions,” he said at a news conference after the decision. “They’ve tightened a bit since we met last time. That isn’t something that we’re uncomfortable with.” He said the goal “isn’t to throw sand in the gears of the economy and throw people out of work.”
At least five of the 12 Federal Reserve districts attributed weaker housing or real estate demand to higher long-term or mortgage rates in the Fed’s October Beige Book, based on information collected through Oct. 5. In Atlanta’s district, some builders said they expect mortgage rate buydowns to become a permanent sales tactic.
The National Association of Home Builders tied last month’s jump in long-term yields to forces beyond Fed policy, including elevated oil prices and geopolitical tension, the federal deficit, weak demand at Treasury auctions and “strong competition for capital from AI and hyperscaler investment.”
Hammack signaled her position two weeks before the meeting. In an Oct. 12 speech in Cleveland, she said a restrictive stance was appropriate to ensure “a timely return to 2 percent inflation.” She also said that with the recent rise in yields, she viewed financial conditions as “neutral rather than holding demand back.”
Fed projections released in September pointed to another quarter-point increase before year-end. Warsh declined to say whether support for another hike this year remains widespread, saying he does not believe in forward guidance outside a crisis.
Inflation ranked among the top three issues for 46% of registered voters in a Center Square Voters’ Voice Poll conducted Oct. 5-7 by Noble Predictive Insights, up nine points since March. The survey of 2,527 registered voters has a margin of error of plus or minus 1.95 percentage points for the full sample. Inflation led among Democrats and Democratic-leaning voters at 47%, Republicans and Republican-leaning voters at 45% and true independents at 48%. Voters go to the polls Nov. 3.

The Federal Open Market Committee approved the action 10–2, according to its statement released Wednesday. Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack dissented because they preferred higher rates, not a reduction.
The committee described economic growth as strong, domestic spending as resilient and investment as robust. It said job growth had kept pace with the workforce and unemployment had changed little. Those assessments accompanied a warning that inflation remained elevated.

Operating rates also unchanged
A separate implementation note keeps interest on reserve balances at 3.90%, effective October 29. The Board of Governors unanimously approved that decision.
The instructions also retain a 4% rate for standing overnight repurchase operations and a 3.75% offering rate for overnight reverse repurchase operations. The primary credit rate remains 4%.

Did the Fed change its benchmark target?
No. The range remains 3.75%–4%.
What was the vote?
10–2.
Who dissented?
Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack.
What did the dissenters want?
A quarter-percentage-point increase.
What is the inflation goal?
The committee reaffirmed its 2% goal.

sources.news_title: Fed Holds Interest Rates Steady at Final Meeting Before Election
sources.text:
by Jack McGeever
The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady Wednesday at its final monetary policy meeting before the midterm elections, despite mounting inflationary pressures that have pushed consumer and wholesale prices sharply higher since September.
The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) maintained its benchmark federal funds rate at a target range of 3.75% to 4.00%, pausing after raising rates by 25 basis points in September for the first time since 2023. The decision came less than a week before voters head to the polls, with inflation and the cost of living ranking among Americans’ top concerns ahead of the elections.
The Fed raised rates by a quarter percentage point on Sept. 16 in a unanimous 12-0 vote, citing persistent inflation and resilient economic activity. Policymakers said the increase would support a faster return to the central bank’s 2% inflation target.
Economic data released in the weeks following that decision showed inflation remained elevated.
The Consumer Price Index (CPI) increased 0.6% in September and 3.7% over the preceding 12 months, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) report released Oct. 14. Gasoline prices surged 9.1% during September, accounting for more than half of the overall monthly increase.
Meanwhile, the Producer Price Index (PPI) jumped 1.3% in September, its largest monthly increase since March 2022, according to data released Oct. 15. Wholesale prices increased 6.3% from a year earlier, marking the largest annual increase since December 2022.
Inflation and the broader economy have emerged as leading issues ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections. An AP-NORC poll released Oct. 15 found that 85% of voters considered the economy one of the most important issues influencing their vote, while 84% said the same about the cost of living.
President Donald Trump previously accused the Federal Reserve of keeping interest rates artificially low to benefit Democrats. During the 2016 presidential campaign, Trump accused then-Fed Chair Janet Yellen of maintaining low rates under political pressure from the Obama administration. Trump later pressured former Fed Chairman Jerome Powell to lower borrowing costs, telling him during a May 2025 meeting that the central bank was making a mistake by refusing to cut rates, according to the White House.
The Fed’s struggle with inflation follows a 2020 policy shift that allowed inflation to run moderately above its 2% target to compensate for years of below-target inflation. Consumer inflation subsequently reached 9.1% in June 2022, and Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh told Congress in April that the central bank’s 2020 decision laid the foundation for the inflation surge Americans experienced in subsequent years.
The consequences of inflation extend beyond rising consumer prices. Unexpected inflation can reduce the real value of existing federal debt, according to research published by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, while simultaneously eroding the purchasing power of Americans’ wages and savings. Wednesday’s decision left borrowing costs unchanged despite inflation remaining above the central bank’s 2% target.
The labor market, however, offered a more mixed picture.
The U.S. economy added just 29,000 jobs in September, while the unemployment rate stood at 4.2%, according to the BLS employment report released Oct. 2. July and August payroll figures were revised downward by a combined 60,000 jobs, underscoring the slowdown in hiring.
Despite weak job creation, initial unemployment claims declined to 194,000 for the week ending Oct. 17, suggesting employers remained hesitant to shed workers even as hiring slowed.
The Fed’s decision to leave borrowing costs unchanged aligned with expectations among economists who anticipated policymakers would wait until December before tightening monetary policy again.
A Reuters poll conducted Oct. 16-20 found that 94 of 100 economists expected the Fed to leave rates unchanged in October, while all 100 anticipated an increase at the central bank’s December meeting.
Higher interest rates can make credit cards, auto loans and other forms of borrowing more expensive, while persistent inflation reduces the purchasing power of household incomes.
– – –
Jack McGeever is a reporter at Daily Caller News Foundation.

sources.news_title: Fed Holds Rates Steady Before Midterms — Lisa Cook Breaks Ranks to Demand a Hike – 100PercentFedUp.com – by Isaac
sources.text:
The Federal Reserve just made its final interest-rate decision before the midterm elections.
And one of the two officials demanding an immediate rate hike was Lisa Cook.
In a 10-2 vote Wednesday, the Fed left its benchmark target range at 3.75% to 4.00%, pausing after September’s quarter-point increase.
Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack broke with the majority. Both wanted another quarter-point hike now.
That is a remarkable split with Election Day only six days away, inflation still punishing American households, and Cook herself facing a White House inquiry over mortgage allegations.
The official announcement came directly from the central bank:
Federal Reserve issues #FOMC statement: https://t.co/D6u2WlUUav
— Federal Reserve (@federalreserve) October 28, 2026
The Federal Reserve voted 10-2 on October 28 to keep the federal funds target range at 3.75% to 4.00%, leaving its policy rate unchanged after September’s quarter-point increase. The statement said economic activity was expanding at a strong pace, supported by resilient domestic spending and robust capital investment, even as inflation remained elevated.
That combination explains why the decision was a hold rather than a declaration that the inflation fight is over. The committee said it needs more information before choosing its next move and remains committed to price stability, leaving another increase possible before the end of the year.
For now, ten members chose to wait for more data, while Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack wanted an immediate quarter-point increase. Their dissent turns the October hold into more than a routine pause: it records a clear split over whether inflation warrants a second consecutive hike just six days before the midterm elections.
Cook’s vote stands out.
She was appointed to the Fed by Joe Biden, and President Trump has been trying to remove her over allegations that she made conflicting statements on mortgage applications.
Cook has not been charged with a crime and denies the mortgage allegations. The inquiry, however, has not changed her vote on the Federal Open Market Committee.
Cook remains one of 12 officials voting on monetary policy that can ripple through credit cards, auto loans, business financing, housing, markets, and the value of every paycheck.
Now, at the most politically sensitive moment on the calendar, she has cast her first dissent as a Federal Reserve official — and it was for higher rates.
Axios reported that Cook had never previously dissented from a Fed policy decision. Hammack, by contrast, has been a consistent inflation hawk and was widely viewed as a likely vote for another increase.
The report said Fed officials may still raise rates before the end of the year, but Chairman Kevin Warsh and the majority want to move gradually while gathering more data.
Axios also noted that the Fed upgraded its description of economic growth from “solid” in September to “strong” in October. That is hardly the language of an economy collapsing under the current rate range.
At the same time, the central bank’s preferred inflation target remains 2%, with current price growth still well above it. The question is whether another hike now would curb inflation or impose more pain before the data justify it.
Warsh took questions after the decision in the Fed’s official press conference:
LIVE NOW: Press conference with #FOMC Chairman Warsh: https://t.co/1uJrua5Yif and https://t.co/FJa6TblbC1
— Federal Reserve (@federalreserve) October 28, 2026
There is another layer to Cook’s dissent that cannot be ignored.
The Associated Press reported earlier this month that President Trump created a committee of inquiry to examine allegations involving Cook’s mortgage applications.
A White House hearing is scheduled for November 5. Cook is expected to have an opportunity to answer the evidence and present her position before the committee makes a recommendation on whether legal cause exists to remove her.
AP reported that Cook denies wrongdoing and has not been charged with a crime. Her attorneys argue that the allegations do not justify her removal.
The same report noted that September’s quarter-point increase passed unanimously, meaning Cook supported the first hike. One meeting later, she joined Hammack in calling for a second consecutive increase while ten other members voted to hold.
The timing alone does not prove a political motive.
The calendar still matters: Cook cast the dissent six days before voters decide control of Congress.
Interest rates are among the most consequential decisions any government institution makes. When a Biden-appointed governor under an active removal inquiry votes to raise them six days before the midterms, Americans are entitled to scrutinize the vote, the data, and the judgment behind it.
Warsh’s written opening statement confirmed the committee’s decision and the range it chose to preserve:
Read Chairman Warsh's full opening statement from the #FOMC press conference (PDF): https://t.co/TPqQ7MKO7m pic.twitter.com/1SUkOfaU0T
— Federal Reserve (@federalreserve) October 28, 2026
The hold does not mean relief is on the way tomorrow.
The federal funds rate does not directly set every consumer loan, and mortgage rates follow longer-term bond markets more closely. But the Fed’s stance still shapes the cost and availability of money throughout the economy.
For families already squeezed by years of higher prices, another rate hike would add a second burden: expensive goods and expensive credit at the same time.
The Fed majority decided that was a step too far without more evidence.
Lisa Cook wanted to take it anyway.
That vote is now part of the record — and voters can judge it for themselves.

sources.news_title: Fed pause won't lower mortgage rates, economists say
sources.text:
(The Center Square) – The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady Wednesday, a decision that does little for homebuyers facing mortgage rates near 7.3% and builder confidence that is at a 14-year low.
The Federal Open Market Committee kept its benchmark rate at 3.75% to 4% on a 10-2 vote, according to the Fed's policy statement. Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented, preferring a quarter-point increase. September's decision was unanimous.
The rate that prices a mortgage is not the one the Fed sets. The 10-year Treasury yield, which mortgage rates track, traded just above 5% Wednesday afternoon, according to Tradeweb data. Freddie Mac put the average 30-year fixed mortgage at 7.32% last week, up from 6.19% a year earlier. That is a gap of more than a full percentage point built up over a year in which the Fed raised short-term rates once.
"For homebuyers, today's decision changes very little," said Orphe Divounguy, The Center Square's economist. "The Fed doesn't directly set mortgage rates. Financial markets do, based on expectations for inflation, economic growth, future interest rates and the risks associated with mortgage-backed securities."
His research found that about half of a change in the 10-year Treasury yield reaches mortgage rates the same day, and about two-thirds within two days.
Builder confidence fell three points to 29 in October, the lowest reading since June 2012, according to the National Association of Home Builders/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index.
Buyer traffic dropped to 18, which National Association of Home Builders Chief Economist Robert Dietz said in the NAHB's Oct. 19 release was the weakest since April 2012, excluding the start of the pandemic. Margins are being compressed by rising costs and incentive use, Dietz told The Center Square.
Forty-three percent of builders cut prices last month, the highest share since 2020, and 65% offered sales incentives.
In written commentary after the decision, Mortgage Bankers Association Chief Economist Mike Fratantoni said rates at three-year highs are "causing a sharp slowdown in home sales, mortgage originations, and in commercial real estate markets."
Although the Fed held Wednesday, he said, markets have already priced in at least two more increases, and "we do not expect any significant relief in mortgage rates over the forecast horizon."
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said tighter financial conditions are how the policy is meant to work.
"The dominant means in which this policy is going to be put into practice is we are tightening financial conditions," he said at a news conference after the decision. "They've tightened a bit since we met last time. That isn't something that we're uncomfortable with." He said the goal "isn't to throw sand in the gears of the economy and throw people out of work."
At least five of the 12 Federal Reserve districts attributed weaker housing or real estate demand to higher long-term or mortgage rates in the Fed's October Beige Book, based on information collected through Oct. 5. In Atlanta's district, some builders said they expect mortgage rate buydowns to become a permanent sales tactic.
The National Association of Home Builders tied last month's jump in long-term yields to forces beyond Fed policy, including elevated oil prices and geopolitical tension, the federal deficit, weak demand at Treasury auctions and "strong competition for capital from AI and hyperscaler investment."
Hammack signaled her position two weeks before the meeting. In an Oct. 12 speech in Cleveland, she said a restrictive stance was appropriate to ensure "a timely return to 2 percent inflation." She also said that with the recent rise in yields, she viewed financial conditions as "neutral rather than holding demand back."
Fed projections released in September pointed to another quarter-point increase before year-end. Warsh declined to say whether support for another hike this year remains widespread, saying he does not believe in forward guidance outside a crisis.
Inflation ranked among the top three issues for 46% of registered voters in a Center Square Voters' Voice Poll conducted Oct. 5-7 by Noble Predictive Insights, up nine points since March. The survey of 2,527 registered voters has a margin of error of plus or minus 1.95 percentage points for the full sample. Inflation led among Democrats and Democratic-leaning voters at 47%, Republicans and Republican-leaning voters at 45% and true independents at 48%. Voters go to the polls Nov. 3.

sources.news_title: Federal Reserve keeps interest rates unchanged
The Fed held rates steady. Smart people in business say they still expect another hike in December.
sources.text:
The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady as was widely expected. The rate remained unchanged after a 10-2 vote, where 2 officials voted to hike rates by 25 bps.
Fed chair Kevin Warsh, who began his term leading the central bank in May, said the Fed is working to deliver future price stability and quash inflation during the Federal Open Market Committee press conference following the hold announcement.
"The period right in front of us is information rich," Warsh said.
He added: "We're going to be able to figure out what's the appropriate protocol, as part of this package that we started to deliver five months ago, to deliver price stability."
In September, the Fed opted for a quarter-point increase — the first hike in three years — aimed at tackling rising inflation. The decision to hold rates comes less than a week before US midterm elections, where the country's affordability crisis and rising energy and oil prices are fresh on voters' minds. Warsh said politics played no role in the decision.
Here is how smart people in business and finance are reacting to the hold — and why many expect another rate hike in December.
Kay Haigh, global head and chief investment officer of fixed income and liquidity solutions at Goldman Sachs Asset Management
Haigh is among the Fed watchers who expect a hike to be the likely outcome of the final Fed meeting of the year.
"We expect the Fed to resume rate hikes in December," Haigh said. "September's strong CPI print is a reminder that upside inflation risks remain, and the Fed is likely to look to take out further insurance."
Steve Rick, chief economist at TruStage
Rick said Wednesday's decision to keep rates steady made sense after September's first hike since July 2023.
"Monetary policy works with long and variable lags, so the Fed will want to see how the higher rates already in the system are affecting consumer spending, business investment and hiring before determining whether additional tightening is necessary," he said. "There's no need to rush."
Andrew Davis, head of investment strategy at Bryn Mawr Trust and a former BLS analyst
Davis said the Fed's wait-and-see approach makes sense as inflation remains above the Fed's 2% target and the job market has cooled without "showing the kind of widespread deterioration we'd typically associate with a recession."
"One thing worth watching is how the bond market responds," Davis said. "The Fed controls short-term interest rates, but longer-term yields reflect a much broader set of forces, including inflation expectations, economic growth and Treasury supply. With the 10-year Treasury yield around 5%, financial conditions have already tightened considerably. Higher borrowing costs can do some of the Fed's work without another rate hike."
Elizabeth Renter, the lead economist at Life360 and a former senior economist at NerdWallet
"The Fed's choice to hold today will have little noticeable impact for everyday household life," she said. "But consumers paying attention could feel let down by the seeming inaction on inflation from the Central Bank."

sources.text:
The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady on Wednesday as the economy faces a monthslong surge of inflation ahead of the midterm elections.
The Fed’s benchmark interest rate currently stands between 3.75% and 4%. That level marks a significant drop from a recent peak attained in 2023, but rates stand well above a 0% level established at the outset of the COVID-19 pandemic.
An acceleration of price increases this year has posed a challenge for Fed officials tasked with containing inflation. The central bank raised interest rates a quarter of a percentage point last month in an effort to battle back price woes. The move marked the first rate increase in three years.
That rate hike should help cool off inflation by slowing the economy and eating away at demand, though such a policy move typically yields results after a lag time lasting several months.
Policymakers may lose patience as they weigh whether the current level of interest rates is high enough to ease price hikes. The odds of a quarter-point rate hike at the Fed’s next meeting in December are pegged at nearly 80%, according to CME Group’s FedWatch Tool, a measure of market sentiment.
In the meantime, price increases are accelerating. Inflation rose to a four-month high in September as fuel prices climbed in response to unrest in the Middle East, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS).
Prices increased 3.7% in September compared to a year earlier, putting the inflation rate more than a percentage point above the Fed’s target level of 2%, data showed.
The rise of inflation may put pressure on the Fed to ratchet up interest rates in an escalation of its fight against price hikes. That policy would mean pressing the brakes harder on the economy — risking sluggish growth and job cuts.
A weak jobs report this month complicated the economic picture, suggesting a resilient labor market may be wobbling more than previously thought.
Employers added 29,000 jobs in September, a sharp slowdown from the 162,000 jobs added in August, the BLS said. The job gains came in well below economists’ expectations.
Economic conditions pose a quandary for the Fed, Bank of America Global Research said in a memo to clients last week.
“If the Fed hikes, investors might worry about overtightening. If the Fed holds, markets could question the Fed’s inflation-fighting credibility,” the memo said.
The rate decision may also thrust the central bank into a political maelstrom in the final sprint to Election Day.
President Donald Trump has repeatedly criticized the Fed for raising interest rates over across both terms in office, including a reprimand leveled at the Fed soon after its rate increase last month.
“LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!” Trump said in a social media post hours after the announcement.
The Fed is an independent institution established by Congress. The central bank is typically insulated from political interference, but several past presidents have sought to influence the Fed’s interest rate policy, including Trump.
The rate decision may also draw attention to the challenge posed by inflation, a top issue among voters.

By Howard Schneider
WASHINGTON, Oct 28 (Reuters) – The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady on Wednesday, as expected, opting to delay any changes to borrowing costs until after next week’s US midterm elections and awaiting further data on the path of inflation.
In a 10-2 decision, the US central bank said it would maintain its benchmark interest rate within the current 3.75%-4.00% range while acknowledging that inflation “remains elevated,” upgrading its assessment of the economy, and hinting that further rate hikes may be coming depending on the performance of inflation.
“The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee’s 2% goal,” the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee said in its latest policy statement. “The Committee will deliver price stability.”
Fed Governor Lisa Cook, currently targeted by President Donald Trump for removal from the central bank, dissented in favor of a quarter-percentage-point rate hike, as did Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, a consistently hawkish voice who also dissented in July for the same reason.
The Fed’s latest policy statement is a notable change from the September 15-16 meeting, with a hint of the sort of forward guidance Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh has said he wants to avoid.
The Fed’s assessment of the economy was upgraded to “strong” from the “solid” expansion seen as of the September meeting, while investment was still viewed as robust and job gains were keeping pace with the workforce.
FEARS THAT INFLATION IS BROADENING
The outcome of this week’s meeting was widely expected after top Fed officials indicated they saw no rush to raise rates again following the quarter-percentage-point increase approved last month, despite inflation data in the meantime that was stronger than forecast and concerns that price pressures are broadening across the economy.
Energy costs remain high, including for diesel fuel, which is a key input for shipping, agriculture, and other industries. Inflation and the cost of living in general have been central to the political races that will determine whether Trump’s Republican Party remains in control of both houses of Congress on November 3, or whether Democrats move into leadership positions and gain more robust oversight powers, including over the Fed.
Warsh will hold a press conference at 2:30 p.m. EDT (1830 GMT) to elaborate on the policy decision and economic outlook.
Investors expect further rate hikes will be needed, beginning in December and continuing into 2027, to lower inflation that is currently around a percentage point above the Fed’s target and has shown little progress in recent months.
The US central bank has missed its inflation target for five and a half years, a fact that has left some officials worried that businesses and households are becoming accustomed to faster price increases and may plan for them in ways that will make inflation harder to control.

WASHINGTON (AP) — The Federal Reserve kept its key rate unchanged Wednesday at about 3.9% despite stubbornly high inflation, while providing little hint about the central bank’s next moves.
“Inflation remains elevated,” the Fed said in a statement released after its two-day policy meeting. Holding off on an increase will allow “the accumulation of more information” that will help determine what policy the Fed should pursue “to ensure a timely return of inflation” to the central bank’s 2% inflation target, the statement said.
The Fed, led by Chairman Kevin Warsh, raised its benchmark rate last month for the first time in three years, defying President Donald Trump’s demands for rate cuts, in an effort to get inflation back to its 2% target in a “timelier” manner. The statement leaves the Fed’s next moves unclear, even though officials last month penciled in another rate hike for this year. Consumers have generally soured on an economy weighed down by more expensive gas, groceries, and clothing, among other items. Yet Warsh faces plenty of challenges in getting inflation back to target. Some of the forces pushing up prices — specifically the rapid buildout of artificial intelligence infrastructure and higher energy prices — won’t easily be tamed by higher interest rates.
Two Fed officials dissented from Wednesday’s decision, with Fed governor Lisa Cook and Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland President Beth Hammack voting in favor of hiking rates by a quarter point. This is Cook’s first dissent since she was appointed to the board by President Joe Biden in 2022.

Higher mortgage rates have made buying a home unaffordable for 5 million more Americans since the beginning of the year, according to Oxford Economics, a consulting firm. Inflation picked up in September, when consumer prices rose 3.7% compared with a year earlier. The increase was much bigger than the 2.4% rate in February, just before the Iran war.

Central banks in Brazil, Mexico and Chile set their own rates, but they follow what the Fed does and says. A US rate that stays put gives them one less shock to manage.

Money sent home from the United States to Mexico, Central America and parts of Africa is paid in dollars. When the dollar and local currencies move against each other, the same transfer buys more or less at home.

The decision does not signal that the Fed has declared victory over inflation. The two dissenters wanted rates higher immediately, and market participants continued to anticipate the possibility of another increase at the December meeting.

Many governments and companies there borrow in dollars, and US rates set the benchmark for that borrowing. They also influence currencies and the flow of investment into emerging markets.

Holding off on an increase will allow “the accumulation of more information” that will help determine what policy the Fed should pursue “to ensure a timely return of inflation” to the central bank’s 2% inflation target, the statement said.
The Fed, led by Chairman Kevin Warsh, raised its benchmark rate last month for the first time in three years, defying President Donald Trump’s demands for rate cuts, in an effort to get inflation back to its 2% target in a “timelier” manner. The Fed is tasked by Congress to combat inflation, and it does so by lifting rates to slow borrowing and spending and cool price increases.
The statement leaves the Fed’s next moves unclear, even though officials last month penciled in another rate hike for this year. Wall Street investors have also priced in a rate hike in December, according to futures markets. Whether the Fed is still leaning toward another hike will likely be a key issue in the news conference held by Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh this afternoon.
The Fed’s decision comes just six days before a midterm election that has focused heavily on concerns around the cost of living and affordability. Consumers have generally soured on an economy weighed down by more expensive gas, groceries, and clothing, among other items. Yet Warsh faces plenty of challenges in getting inflation back to target. Some of the forces pushing up prices — specifically the rapid buildout of artificial intelligence infrastructure and higher energy prices — won’t easily be tamed by higher interest rates.
Two Fed officials dissented from Wednesday’s decision, with Fed governor Lisa Cook and Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland President Beth Hammack voting in favor of hiking rates by a quarter point. This is Cook’s first dissent since she was appointed to the board by President Joe Biden in 2022.
Cook has been targeted by the Trump administration, which tried to fire her last year, though the Supreme Court in June ruled she could keep her job while litigation played out. No president has fired a Fed governor before, a sign of the Fed’s longstanding independence from day-to-day politics. Trump renewed his attempt to remove Cook last month by setting up a committee to look into allegations Cook committed mortgage fraud, which she has denied.
President Trump has also slammed the Fed for raising its key rate last month, though he largely blamed the central bank's rate-setting committee, rather than Warsh, whom he appointed.
Other parts of the economy are already being hit by higher rates, which were lifted by market forces, even before the Fed hiked last month. The average 30-year mortgage rate reached a three-year high of 7.4% earlier this month, though it has since slipped a bit. Higher mortgage rates have made buying a home unaffordable for 5 million more Americans since the beginning of the year, according to Oxford Economics, a consulting firm. Over time, Fed rate hikes can make mortgages, auto loans, and credit card borrowing more expensive, adding to Americans' sense that things like homes and cars are getting pricier.
Inflation picked up in September, when consumer prices rose 3.7% compared with a year earlier. The increase was much bigger than the 2.4% rate in February, just before the Iran war.
And on a monthly basis, the consumer price index — the most widely followed inflation gauge — rose 0.3% in both August and September. At that pace over a full year, inflation would rise much more quickly than the Fed's 2% target.
A separate inflation measure more closely followed by the Fed, the personal consumption expenditures price index, comes out Thursday and is forecast to have jumped 3.6% in September from a year earlier, up from 3.4% in August. Core prices, which exclude the food and energy categories, are forecast to have risen 3.1%, up from 3% the previous month.
The Fed's policy meeting is part of a busy week for central banks around the world. The Bank of Canada will also meet Wednesday and is forecast to lift its key rate a quarter point, to 2.5%. Policymakers at the European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan are both scheduled to meet Thursday and are expected to keep their key rates unchanged.
For Warsh and the Fed, another key consideration is that the U.S. economy is growing at a healthy pace and unemployment remains low, at 4.2%, even if hiring is also sluggish. The government will report Thursday on growth for the July-September quarter, which is expected to reach 3%, according to a forecast by data provider FactSet. That would be up from 2.2% in the April-June quarter.
Many economists argue that solid growth is evidence that interest rates aren't particularly high and the economy could withstand higher rates to combat inflation.

sources.text:
US Fed keeps rates unchanged despite elevated inflation
The Federal Reserve has kept its key rate unchanged at about 3.9 per cent despite elevated inflation while providing little hint about the US central bank's next moves.
"Inflation remains elevated," the Fed said in a statement released after its two-day policy meeting.
Holding off on an increase will allow "the accumulation of more information" that will help determine what policy the Fed should pursue "to ensure a timely return of inflation" to the central bank's 2.0 per cent inflation target, the statement said.
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh expressed confidence US inflation can be lowered to the two per cent target without having to "throw sand in the gears" and slow growth or raise unemployment.
Warsh, speaking at a press conference, said he expects a report on third-quarter gross domestic product on Thursday to show strong investment and consumer spending and an acceleration of growth from the first half of the year.
Warsh, however, said he still does not think the US economy is "too hot" or generating demand-side inflation that needs to be curbed.
"The economy is pointing in the right direction. Is the economy running too hot? Is the economy running too strong? That isn't the judgment of most of my colleagues," said Warsh, arguing, as he has before, that changes in productivity, even predating the artificial intelligence boom, may allow the US to grow faster without as much inflation.
"The goal, in my view ... isn't to throw sand in the gears of the economy and throw people out of work. I don't think we have to do that."
Rather, Warsh said, a higher Fed policy rate is already showing its impact in slightly tighter credit conditions that could, for example, slow business investment and which arguably contributed to recent stock market declines, another potential source of "disinflation" if it slows spending among wealthier families.
Last month the Fed raised its benchmark rate for the first time in three years, defying US President Donald Trump's demands for rate cuts, in an effort to get inflation back to its 2.0 per cent target in a "timelier" manner.
In comments to CNBC on Thursday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the Trump administration continues to have faith that Warsh will "find the right balance" between the two per cent inflation goal and continuing economic growth.
Two Fed officials dissented from Wednesday's decision, with Fed governor Lisa Cook and Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland president Beth Hammack voting in favour of hiking rates by a quarter point.

ASX rises, Fed keeps rates on hold despite inflation surge
Updated ,first published
The Australian sharemarket has made a bright start to the session on the back of a positive lead from Wall Street after the Federal Reserve, as expected, kept interest rates on hold.
The S&P/ASX 200 was up 38.8 points, or 0.4 per cent, to 8886.1 in early trade. Wall Street closed in positive territory after the Federal Reserve opted to delay any changes to borrowing costs until after next week’s US midterm elections and awaiting further data on the path of inflation. The Australian dollar was trading at US70.49¢.
After strong gains overnight, oil prices dipped in early Asian trade as traders weighed fresh diplomatic efforts in the Middle East to avert a potential restart of US military strikes on Iran. West Texas Intermediate fell toward $US102 a barrel, after rising almost 3 per cent in the previous session, while Brent closed near $US115. Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said that Tehran continued to give diplomacy a chance, and the Wall Street Journal reported US Vice President JD Vance had reached out to Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of the nation’s top security body.
President Donald Trump told Axios that negotiations were taking place through mediators but stressed he didn’t know whether they would bear fruit. “We need to finish the job – either through a deal or another way – we will find out if negotiations can succeed,” he was quoted as saying.
Energy stocks are higher on the ASX, with Woodside Energy up 1.1 per cent, Santos rising 1 per cent and refiner Ampol adding 0.8 per cent in early trade.
Financial stocks advanced across the board with National Australia Bank and Westpac up 1.3 per cent while Commonwealth Bank added 0.7 per cent and ANZ Bank rose 0.6 per cent.
Wesfarmers lost 2.9 per cent after releasing a quarterly update, with the retail giant flagging slowing sales at hardware powerhouse Bunnings. JB HiFi was up 0.8 per cent after releasing its quarterly update, with sales slipping at its Australian stores but rising in New Zealand.
Mining stocks are mixed with Fortescue rising 0.5 per cent, BHP flat and Rio Tinto slid 0.6 per cent. Gold miners rose after the price of the precious metal erased losses after the Fed decision to hover around $US4050 an ounce. Northern Star and Evolution Mining per cent are 0.5 per cent higher in early trade.
Technology stocks are mixed with WiseTech adding 0.6 per cent and Xero up 0.2 per cent but Codan slid 0.2 per cent lower.
On Wall Street, the S&P 500 rose 0.3 per cent, the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 0.2 per cent and the Nasdaq composite rose 0.3 per cent. In the bond market, the two-year Treasury yield initially jumped after the Fed announcement, but reversed course after traders pared expectations for coming hikes to rates.
In a 10-2 decision, the Fed said it would maintain its benchmark interest rate within the current 3.75 per cent-4.00 per cent range while acknowledging that inflation “remains elevated,” upgrading its assessment of the economy, and hinting that further rate hikes may be coming depending on the performance of inflation.
“The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee’s 2 per cent goal,” the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee said in its latest policy statement. “The Committee will deliver price stability.”
At a news conference following the announcement, chair Kevin Warsh said the Fed has “started to see some changes in financial and credit conditions. They have tightened for some businesses and households.”
The Fed raised its benchmark rate last month for the first time in three years, defying President Donald Trump’s demands for rate cuts, in an effort to get inflation back to its 2 per cent target in a “timelier” manner. The Fed is tasked by Congress to combat inflation, and it does so by lifting rates to slow borrowing and spending and cool price increases. The statement leaves the Fed’s next moves unclear, even though officials last month penciled in another rate hike for this year. Wall Street investors have also priced in a rate hike in December, according to futures markets.
Fed Governor Lisa Cook, currently targeted by President Donald Trump for removal from the central bank, dissented in favour of a quarter-percentage-point rate hike, as did Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, a consistently hawkish voice who also dissented in July for the same reason.
Wall Street cares so much about interest rates because they are one of the main levers that set prices for stocks. The other big variable is how much profit companies are making, and several companies rallied Wednesday after joining the list of those beating analysts’ expectations for the summer.
Etsy climbed 5.5 per cent after its profit for the latest quarter blew past analysts’ forecasts. CEO Kruti Patel Goyal said the online marketplace saw growth in active buyers from prior-year levels for the first time in two years, while its active seller base grew at its fastest rate in two years.
Stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry were also relatively solid with Micron Technology the strongest force lifting the S&P 500 with a 5.9 per cent gain. But after the closing bell, Alphabet reported a higher cash burn than analysts expected as it spends heavily to boost capacity for its cloud business, sending its shares down more than 6 per cent in extended trading.
Outside of tech and earnings, Wendy’s soared 15.2 per cent to $US7.07 after Trian Fund Management, run by investor Nelson Peltz, offered to buy the chain for $US7.35 per share in cash.

Federal Reserve keeps rates unchanged despite high inflation
Decision comes days before midterm elections that are focused on cost of living
Associated Press
Key Takeaways:
- The Federal Reserve kept its key rate unchanged Oct. 28 at about 3.9% as inflation remained elevated.
- Consumer prices rose 3.7% in September from a year earlier, well above the Fed’s 2% inflation target.
- Two Fed officials favored a quarter-point hike, while markets priced in another increase in December and the Fed offered little guidance.
WASHINGTON — The Federal Reserve kept its key rate unchanged Oct. 28 at about 3.9% despite elevated inflation, while providing little hint about the central bank’s next moves.
“Inflation remains elevated,” the Fed said in a statement released after its two-day policy meeting. Holding off on an increase will allow “the accumulation of more information” that will help determine what policy the Fed should pursue “to ensure a timely return of inflation” to the central bank’s 2% inflation target, the statement said.
The Fed, led by Chairman Kevin Warsh, raised its benchmark rate last month for the first time in three years, defying President Donald Trump’s demands for rate cuts, in an effort to get inflation back to its 2% target in a “timelier” manner. The Fed is tasked by Congress to combat inflation, and it does so by lifting rates to slow borrowing and spending and cool price increases.
The statement leaves the Fed’s next moves unclear, even though officials last month penciled in another rate hike for this year. Wall Street investors have also priced in a rate hike in December, according to futures markets. Whether the Fed is still leaning toward another hike will likely be a key issue in the news conference held by Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh this afternoon.
The Fed’s decision comes just six days before a midterm election that has focused heavily on concerns around the cost of living and affordability. Consumers have generally soured on an economy weighed down by more expensive gas, groceries, and clothing, among other items. Yet Warsh faces plenty of challenges in getting inflation back to target. Some of the forces pushing up prices — specifically the rapid buildout of artificial intelligence infrastructure and higher energy prices — won’t easily be tamed by higher interest rates.

Two Fed officials dissented from the decision, with Fed governor Lisa Cook and Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland President Beth Hammack voting in favor of hiking rates by a quarter point. This is Cook’s first dissent since she was appointed to the board by President Joe Biden in 2022.
Cook has been targeted by the Trump administration, which tried to fire her last year, though the Supreme Court in June ruled she could keep her job while litigation played out. No president has fired a Fed governor before, a sign of the Fed’s longstanding independence from day-to-day politics. Trump renewed his attempt to remove Cook last month by setting up a committee to look into allegations Cook committed mortgage fraud, which she has denied.
President Trump has also slammed the Fed for raising its key rate last month, though he largely blamed the central bank's rate-setting committee, rather than Warsh, whom he appointed.
Other parts of the economy are already being hit by higher rates, which were lifted by market forces, even before the Fed hiked last month. The average 30-year mortgage rate reached a three-year high of 7.4% earlier this month, though it has since slipped a bit. Higher mortgage rates have made buying a home unaffordable for 5 million more Americans since the beginning of the year, according to Oxford Economics, a consulting firm. Over time, Fed rate hikes can make mortgages, auto loans and credit card borrowing more expensive, adding to Americans' sense that things like homes and cars are getting pricier.
Inflation picked up in September, when consumer prices rose 3.7% compared with a year earlier. The increase was much bigger than the 2.4% rate in February, just before the Iran war.

And on a monthly basis, the consumer price index — the most widely followed inflation gauge — rose 0.3% in both August and September. At that pace over a full year, inflation would rise much more quickly than the Fed's 2% target.
A separate inflation measure more closely followed by the Fed, the personal consumption expenditures price index, comes out Oct. 29 and is forecast to have jumped 3.6% in September from a year earlier, up from 3.4% in August. Core prices, which exclude the food and energy categories, are forecast to have risen 3.1%, up from 3% the previous month.
The Fed's policy meeting is part of a busy week for central banks around the world. The Bank of Canada will also meet Oct. 28 and is forecast to lift its key rate a quarter point, to 2.5%. Policymakers at the European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan are both scheduled to meet Oct. 29 and are expected to keep their key rates unchanged.

Federal Reserve Maintains Interest Rates Ahead of the Midterms
sources.text:
The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady on Wednesday in the committee’s last move before the midterm elections, which have been dominated by affordability concerns.
“While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient,” the Federal Open Market Committee said in a statement.
The committee voted 10-2 to maintain rates at 3.75% to 4%. The members cited strong productivity growth and capital investment, as well as job gains, in their decision, their second to last of the year. The two dissenting committee members, Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack, wanted to raise interest rates a quarter percentage point.
In September, the Fed raised rates a quarter percentage point to tamp down on inflation — its first rate hike since 2023. The higher target range, which influences rates for consumer and business loans, sent average mortgage rates climbing to 7.32% for a 30-year loan, according to Freddie Mac. sources.text:
By Howard Schneider and Ann Saphir
WASHINGTON, Oct 28 (Reuters) – The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady on Wednesday, as expected, opting to delay any changes to borrowing costs until after next week’s US midterm elections while it awaits further data on inflation, which the central bank said “remains elevated.”
The 10-2 decision to maintain the Fed’s benchmark interest rate within the 3.75%-4.00% range came with an upgraded assessment of an economy that the central bank now says is growing at a “strong pace.” Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh also expressed confidence that inflation can be lowered to the 2% target without having to “throw sand in the gears” and slow growth or raise unemployment.
Warsh, speaking at a press conference after the end of a two-day policy meeting, said he expects a report on third-quarter gross domestic product on Thursday to show strong investment and consumer spending and an acceleration of growth from the first half of the year. Warsh, however, said he still does not think the economy is “too hot” or generating demand-side inflation that needs to be curbed.
“The economy is pointing in the right direction. Is the economy running too hot? Is the economy running too strong? That isn’t the judgment of most of my colleagues,” said Warsh, arguing, as he has before, that changes in productivity, even predating the artificial intelligence boom, may allow the US to grow faster without as much inflation.
“The goal, in my view … isn’t to throw sand in the gears of the economy and throw people out of work. I don’t think we have to do that.”
Rather, he said, a higher Fed policy rate is already showing its impact in slightly tighter credit conditions that could, for example, slow business investment and which arguably contributed to recent stock market declines, another potential source of “disinflation” if it slows spending among wealthier families.
In comments to CNBC on Thursday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the administration continues to have faith that Warsh will “find the right balance” between the 2% inflation goal and continuing economic growth.
The rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee’s latest policy statement, however, hinted that more rate hikes may be needed, and some of Warsh’s colleagues have been explicit in their concerns that demand, fueled by AI and healthy consumer spending, is starting to drive prices higher.
Between now and the next policy meeting in December, “the accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee’s 2% goal,” the FOMC said. “The Committee will deliver price stability.”
TWO FED POLICYMAKERS DISSENT
Fed Governor Lisa Cook, currently being targeted by President Donald Trump for removal from the central bank, cast her first dissent on a central bank policy decision on Wednesday, favoring a quarter-percentage-point rate hike. Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, a consistently hawkish voice, also dissented in favor of a rate increase.
Market reaction was muted, with US stocks paring gains slightly after the decision but ending higher on the day. Longer-dated US Treasury yields extended their rise. Short-term interest-rate futures rose a bit, as traders scaled back a bit on bets of Fed rate hikes ahead.
“The forces keeping the Federal Reserve hawkish haven’t faded. Diesel and gasoline prices remain elevated, AI-driven inflation isn’t easing, and the labor market remains resilient,” said Michael Pearce, chief US economist at Oxford Economics.
The outcome of this week’s meeting was widely expected after top Fed officials indicated they saw no rush to raise rates again following the quarter-percentage-point increase approved last month, despite inflation data in the meantime that was stronger than forecast and concerns that price pressures are broadening across the economy.
Energy costs remain high, including for diesel fuel, which is a key input for shipping, agriculture and other industries. Inflation and the cost of living in general have been central to the political races that will determine whether Trump’s Republican Party remains in control of both houses of Congress on November 3, or whether Democrats move into leadership positions and gain more robust oversight powers, including over the Fed.
Trump, during his first and second terms in the White House, has excoriated the Fed for failing to deliver big rate cuts. After its decision in September to raise rates, he blamed Warsh’s policymaking colleagues as “hostile” and “partisan.”
Warsh told reporters on Wednesday that politics played no role in the decision to leave rates unchanged this week, rebutting, at least indirectly, Trump’s allegation of central bank bias.
Financial markets are still pricing in a couple of additional rate hikes in the coming months, though with slightly less conviction than before Warsh spoke on Wednesday. Pricing shows about an 80% chance of a rate hike at the Fed’s December 8-9 meeting, with another increase in borrowing costs likely by March.
Inflation, which is currently around a percentage point above the Fed’s target, has shown little progress in recent months.
The US central bank has missed its inflation target for more than half a decade, a fact that has left some officials worried that businesses and households are becoming accustomed to faster price increases and may plan for them in ways that will make inflation harder to control.
(Reporting by Howard Schneider and Michael S. Derby; Additional reporting by Ann Saphir and Michael S. Derby; Editing by Paul Simao)
