sources.news_title: Federal Reserve Leaves Interest Rates Unchanged
sources.text:
The Federal Reserve left interest rates unchanged at its October policy meeting, despite ongoing inflation concerns.
In a widely expected decision, the Federal Open Market Committee voted 10–2 to keep the benchmark federal funds rate in the current target range of 3.75 percent to 4 percent on Oct. 28, “in support of the Federal Reserve’s dual mandate.”
Fed board member Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack were the lone dissenters, preferring to raise interest rates by a quarter point.
“Economic activity is expanding at a strong pace,” the central bank said in a post-meeting statement.
“While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient. Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust. Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little.”
This marked Cook’s first dissent since joining the central bank as an appointee of President Joe Biden in 2022.
The last time the rate-setting committee left rates unchanged this past summer, Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan and Minneapolis Fed President Neel Kashkari dissented with Hammack.
With the midterm elections days away, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh reaffirmed the central bank’s independence, adding that officials did not take politics into account.
“I just spent two days with my colleagues upstairs. I didn’t hear an utterance about politics,” Warsh said. “I didn’t hear a reference to politics, elections, what’s happening in the next week or so.”
Market Reaction
U.S. stocks barely reacted to the news, with the leading benchmark averages little changed.
“This was really no surprise. The general view is that the Fed is raising rates but doing so at a slower pace and alternating meetings,” Larry Holzenthaler, senior portfolio manager at Catalyst Funds, told The Epoch Times in an emailed note.
Yields on U.S. Treasury bonds were mixed. The benchmark 10-year yield firmed above 5 percent, while the 30-year ticked up to about 5.33 percent.
The two-year yield, which tracks Fed policy expectations, rose to about 4.78 percent.
The U.S. dollar index—a gauge of the greenback against a weighted basket of currencies—was flat at about 102.30.
Economists at Dutch bank ING have penciled in a quarter-point boost to the federal funds rate in December, “followed by a prolonged pause through to December 2027.”
“Our forecast path for the Fed assumes that in the couple of months following the midterm elections we see an agreement that improves the flow of energy from the Persian Gulf, but significantly, also allows for a sharp reduction in shipping and insurance costs,” they said in an Oct. 23 research note.
Schedule Adjustment
The Fed will be making fewer interest rate decisions next year.
Warsh said that the central bank will adjust its meeting schedule in 2027 and 2028. While the rate-setting committee will still meet eight times per year, one of those meetings in 2027 will center primarily on strategy. In 2028, there will be two strategy sessions.
According to the central bank chief, it is about making the right policy decisions by thinking long-term.
“Getting policy right involves assessing near-term developments at timely, regular, and information-rich intervals,” he said.
“But it’s equally important we reserve time and space as an intellectually diverse group for strategic deliberations, for thinking anew about big questions, looking out over longer time horizons, focusing, as I say, on the left side of the decimal point.”
Global Policy Decisions
After what Warsh characterized as “synchronous tightening” across the major central banks last month, monetary authorities could still maintain a hawkish stance heading into 2027.
While the Bank of Japan is expected to hold rates at 1.25 percent this week, a CNBC survey of economists and strategists suggested that Tokyo could set the stage for a December rate hike.
Futures markets also suggest that the Bank of England could follow through on a 25-basis-point move at next week’s meeting.
Economic observers have debated whether this tightening is necessary, since raising interest rates cannot reverse the war-driven oil-price shock. But rate hikes can also help prevent second- and third-order inflation effects from filtering through the economy.
“The Bank [of Canada] appears focused on preventing elevated oil prices from translating into broader price pressures, with the 2022 oil-driven inflation spike still very much in the rear-view mirror,” David-Alexandre Brassard, chief economist at Chartered Professional Accountants of Canada, said in a statement to The Epoch Times.
Warsh noted that the Fed has observed changes in tighter financial conditions since the September meeting, which could help carve a path toward price stability.
“We have started to see some changes in financial and credit conditions; they have tightened for some businesses and households, much as we would expect,” he told reporters. “Market participants are becoming somewhat more discerning in their capital allocations.”
The Fed’s decision comes one day before a batch of data offers a snapshot of the economy’s health.
September’s personal consumption expenditure price index, third-quarter gross domestic product, and weekly jobless claims will be published on Oct. 29.

sources.text:
The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady Wednesday despite persistent inflation, as policymakers weighed the risk of raising borrowing costs just six days before the midterm elections.
The decision leaves the central bank’s benchmark interest rate unchanged at 3.75% to 4%, following a quarter-point increase in September. That increase was the Fed’s first rate hike in three years.
Wednesday’s decision was widely expected by financial markets, particularly given its proximity to the midterms. While no formal rule prevents the Fed from raising rates immediately before an election, policymakers have historically been reluctant to do so to avoid appearing to have political motivations.

But with the annual inflation at 3.7%, well above the Fed’s 2% target, Wednesday’s move looks more like a pause than a resolution to rising prices. Investors and economists now anticipate a rate hike in December.
In a statement announcing the decision, the Federal Open Market Committee acknowledged that “inflation remains elevated,” but said that this “policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee’s 2 percent goal.”
The decision was approved by a vote of 10 to 2, with Lisa D. Cook and Beth M. Hammack favoring a quarter percentage point raise in the federal funds rate.
Balancing act
The Fed faces an increasingly difficult balancing act. Raising rates could help slow inflation by discouraging borrowing and spending, but it also risks weakening economic growth and employment.
And with Americans already struggling with high prices, higher borrowing costs could add to the financial strain.
“The Fed is moving with caution as opposed to the conviction we saw in 2022,” wrote Diane Swonk, chief economist at KPMG, in a note shared with Straight Arrow. “It does not want to risk a more consequential slowdown to derail a persistent but more subdued bout of inflation than we saw back then.”
Still, inflation is moving in the wrong direction. Wednesday’s decision comes after a series of economic reports that show prices continuing to climb.
Consumer prices rose 0.6% from August to September, and annual inflation jumped from 3.4% to 3.7% last month, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
The war in Iran has continued to disrupt global energy supplies, driving up fuel prices and raising transportation costs for businesses and consumers. Gasoline prices shot up 9.1% in just one month.
But the inflation problem now extends well beyond energy. Core prices, excluding volatile food and energy costs, rose 2.6% in September from a year earlier.
“The data going into December is likely to show hotter inflation,” Swonk wrote, “as the effects of diesel costs make their way into consumer prices.”
Next steps
Looking ahead, policymakers will be closely watching the next release of the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index, the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, for further evidence of whether price pressures are easing or remaining stubbornly elevated.
The Fed’s next rate decision is scheduled for Dec. 9 during its final meeting of the year.

“The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee’s 2 percent goal,” the committee wrote.
In his most drastic change at the central bank yet, Warsh announced that he will be reducing the number of policy votes the Fed holds each year.
Central bankers will still meet eight times a year, but starting in 2027, one of those meetings will not include a vote on interest rates. In 2028, two of those meetings will forgo a vote on rates.
Warsh has argued that fewer votes give policymakers more time to gather data between meetings. Critics have argued that would also makes the Fed slower to react to changes in the economy. The central bank is able to call emergency votes, though these are rare.
Though Warsh remained tight-lipped throughout the press conference, traders priced in 85% odds of a quarter-point hike at the December meeting, according to CME FedWatch.
“Although the Fed held off on raising rates today, as we expected, they left plenty of clues that they were planning to raise rates in December,” Chris Zaccarelli, chief investment officer for Northlight Asset Management, said in a Wednesday note.
“As always, a lot can change in the data between now and then, but if it weren’t so close to the midterm elections, they probably would have raised rates today, and now it’s unlikely that anything will stop them from raising rates at the next meeting.”

"The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2% goal," the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee said in its latest policy statement. "The Committee will deliver price stability."

The Fed's assessment of the economy was upgraded to "strong" from the "solid" expansion seen as of the September meeting, while investment was still viewed as robust and job gains were keeping pace with the workforce.

sources.news_title: Fed Holds Rates Steady Amid Strong Expansion and Elevated Inflation
sources.text:
The Federal Reserve held its benchmark interest rate steady on Wednesday.
The decision keeps the federal funds rate at a range of between 3.75 percent and 4.0 percent, the range set at its previous meeting in September.
“Economic activity is expanding at a strong pace. While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient. Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust. Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little,” the Fed said in a statement at the conclusion of its two-day meeting. “Inflation remains elevated.”
Two Fed officials, Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, dissented from the decision, preferring to raise the target range for the federal funds rate by one-quarter of a percentage point.
At a press conference on Wednesday, Fed chair Kevin Warsh announced a significant change to the Fed’s meetings. Beginning next year, one of the Fed’s eight meetings will be focused on broader economic questions and monetary strategy rather than directly considering the Fed’s policy rates. After that meeting, the Fed would not issue a post-meeting statement, Warsh said. Warsh added that he expects that the strategy meetings will expand to twice a year in 2028.
The September increase was the first increase in three years. The move marked a reversal of the Fed’s previous rounds of cuts in late 2024 and 2025, moves that were spurred by concerns among Fed officials that the economy was slowing and the labor market was weakening. The increase indicated that Fed officials are now confident in the resilience of the economy and view stubborn inflation as a greater risk.
The Fed says it targets two percent inflation. In the pre-pandemic era, inflation consistently undershot that target. Since March of 2021, inflation has run above the target.
The personal consumption expenditures price index, the gauge the Fed favors to measure inflation, was up 3.4 percent in August, the latest month for which the index has been released. It rose by the same amount in July, which was down from the June reading of 3.5 percent and the May reading of 3.8 percent. The September reading is due out Thursday.
Higher gasoline prices have pushed up inflation this year. In recent months, however, inflationary pressures have begun to show up in a broader swath of prices, raising concerns that inflation might be becoming more entrenched.
The decision to leave the benchmark unchanged was widely anticipated by investors. Earlier this week, the futures market was pricing in a 90 percent chance that the Fed kept the federal funds rate steady.
Several Fed officials have signaled that they expect the Fed to raise rates at the December meeting. The CME Group’s FedWatch tool, which tracks the fed funds futures market, says the market implies around an 88 percent chance of a hike at that meeting.
The Fed upgraded its assessment of economic growth, describing activity as expanding at a “strong pace,” compared with the “solid pace” cited in September. The central bank also reiterated its assessments that consumer spending has been resilient, productivity growth is strong, capital investment is robust, and employment has kept pace with the growing workforce. The upbeat description suggests Fed officials see little evidence that higher interest rates are undermining the expansion, potentially giving them greater latitude to tighten monetary policy further to bring down inflation.

sources.news_title: Federal Reserve keeps rates unchanged despite elevated inflation, gives little signal of its next move
sources.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Federal Reserve kept its key rate unchanged Wednesday at about 3.9% despite stubbornly high inflation, while providing little hint about the central bank’s next moves.
“Inflation remains elevated,” the Fed said in a statement released after its two-day policy meeting. Holding off on an increase will allow “the accumulation of more information” that will help determine what policy the Fed should pursue “to ensure a timely return of inflation” to the central bank’s 2% inflation target, the statement said.
The Fed, led by Chairman Kevin Warsh, raised its benchmark rate last month for the first time in three years, defying President Donald Trump’s demands for rate cuts, in an effort to get inflation back to its 2% target in a “timelier” manner. The Fed is tasked by Congress to combat inflation, and it does so by lifting rates to slow borrowing and spending and cool price increases. The statement leaves the Fed’s next moves unclear, even though officials last month penciled in another rate hike for this year. Wall Street investors have also priced in a rate hike in December, according to futures markets.
The Fed’s decision comes just six days before a midterm election that has focused heavily on concerns around the cost of living and affordability. Consumers have generally soured on an economy weighed down by more expensive gas, groceries, and clothing, among other items. Warsh denied the election played a part in the Fed’s staying pat.
“Politics played no role in the decision," he said at a news conference following the announcement. “I just spent two days with my colleagues upstairs. I didn’t hear an utterance about politics.”
Warsh faces plenty of challenges in getting inflation back to target. Some of the forces pushing up prices — specifically the rapid buildout of artificial intelligence infrastructure and higher energy prices — won’t easily be tamed by higher interest rates. Still, Warsh said the Fed has “started to see some changes in financial and credit conditions. They have tightened for some businesses and households," which factored into the decision to keep rates steady.
Parts of the economy are being hit by higher rates, which were lifted by market forces, even before the Fed hiked last month. The average 30-year mortgage rate reached a three-year high of 7.4% earlier this month, though it has since slipped a bit. Higher mortgage rates have made buying a home unaffordable for 5 million more Americans since the beginning of the year, according to Oxford Economics, a consulting firm. Over time, Fed rate hikes can make mortgages, auto loans, and credit card borrowing more expensive, adding to Americans’ sense that things like homes and cars are getting pricier.
A separate inflation measure more closely followed by the Fed, the personal consumption expenditures price index, comes out Thursday and is forecast to have jumped 3.6% in September from a year earlier, up from 3.4% in August. Core prices, which exclude the food and energy categories, are forecast to have risen 3.1%, up from 3% the previous month. Earlier this month, the consumer price index showed inflation picked up in September, when consumer prices rose 3.7% compared with a year earlier.
Warsh denied that consumers would lose faith in the Fed’s ability to get inflation back to its 2% target, given its decision to forego a rate hike.
“There is no soft inflation target," he said.
Two Fed officials dissented from Wednesday’s decision, with Fed governor Lisa Cook and Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland President Beth Hammack voting in favor of hiking rates by a quarter point. This is Cook’s first dissent since she was appointed to the board by President Joe Biden in 2022.
Cook has been targeted by the Trump administration, which tried to fire her last year, though the Supreme Court in June ruled she could keep her job while litigation played out. No president has fired a Fed governor before, a sign of the Fed’s longstanding independence from day-to-day politics. Trump renewed his attempt to remove Cook last month by setting up a committee to look into allegations Cook committed mortgage fraud, which she has denied.
President Trump has also slammed the Fed for raising its key rate last month, though he largely blamed the central bank's rate-setting committee, rather than Warsh, whom he appointed.
The Fed's policy meeting is part of a busy week for central banks around the world. The Bank of Canada will also meet Wednesday and is forecast to lift its key rate a quarter point, to 2.5%. Policymakers at the European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan are both scheduled to meet Thursday and are expected to keep their key rates unchanged.
For Warsh and the Fed, another key consideration is that the U.S. economy is growing at a healthy pace and unemployment remains low, at 4.2%, even if hiring is also sluggish. Warsh said growth in the July-September quarter likely rose above 3%. That would be up from 2.2% in the April-June quarter.
Many economists argue that solid growth is evidence that interest rates aren't particularly high and the economy could withstand higher rates to combat inflation.

sources.news_title: Fed’s pause is a dangerous gamble with world’s largest economy
sources.text:
The Federal Reserve’s decision to hold interest rates days before the midterms is a dangerous gamble with inflation, warns the CEO of deVere Group, one of the world’s largest independent financial advisory organisations.
The comments from Nigel Green come as the Fed holds rates at 3.75% to 4%, with inflation at 3.7% and voters heading to the polls on November 3.
He says: “Prices are rising at almost twice the Fed’s target, and it’s chosen to sit on its hands.
“We’ve been here before, and it ended badly.
“We believe the Fed will likely have to hike again before the year is out anyway. So why wait it out?
“Stalling for the midterms, which is what has happened, we assume, makes no sense when the world’s largest economy is on the line.”
In 2021 the Fed insisted inflation was transitory and kept rates at rock bottom. By the time it finally moved in March 2022, prices were already rising at close to 8%.
Three months later inflation hit 9.1%, a 40-year high. What followed was brutal: four straight hikes of 0.75 percentage points, and rates above 5% by mid-2023.
“The Fed was asleep at the wheel, and families paid for it at the checkout, at the pump and on their mortgages,” comments Nigel Green.
“It took two painful years to rebuild credibility. Throwing that away somehow seems reckless.”
The warning signs are flashing again. The Fed has missed its 2% target for more than five years.
Consumer prices jumped 0.6% in September alone. Core PCE, the Fed’s favoured measure, is heading towards 3.1%. Americans’ fears about prices over the coming year are at their highest since May 2023.
“Energy, tariffs, and the AI building boom are all pushing prices the same way,” he says. “None of it is going away by itself.”
There’s no jobs crisis to hide behind either. Unemployment has held steady at around 4.2% for a year.
“The labour market is solid and inflation is too high. Those are textbook conditions for a hike,” says the deVere CEO.
“If raising rates was right in September, it’s right today. The only thing that’s changed is how close we are to an election.”
Bond markets are losing patience. The 10-year Treasury yield is hovering near 5% after hitting its highest level since 2002 this month, while the average 30-year mortgage rate is close to 7.4%.
“If the Fed won’t tighten, bond investors will do it for them, and they’re far less gentle,” he says.
The timing could hardly be worse, with the White House again trying to oust Fed Governor Lisa Cook despite an earlier Supreme Court setback.
“Independence is everything for a central bank,” says Nigel Green. “Any decision that looks political chips away at it, whatever the motive.”
He concludes: “Kevin Warsh talks tough on inflation. But after the pause, December is now when he has to prove it.
“A firm move then would likely restore confidence fast, and this week’s wobble would soon be forgotten.”
